name: The Prince
info: The Prince is a political treatise by the Italian diplomat Niccolò Machiavelli, written from 1513 as an instruction guide for new princes and printed in 1532; it broke with classical political philosophy and made his name a byword.

facts.made: Niccolò Machiavelli, Italian diplomat and political philosopher, writing in 1513 after the Medici regained Florence; dedicated to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici
facts.form: A short political treatise in the style of the mirrors for princes, in 26 chapters after a dedicatory letter; original Latin title De Principatibus, later Il Principe
facts.where: Read in printed editions and translations; no manuscript in Machiavelli's own handwriting survives
facts.known: The advice that it is safer to be feared than loved; the lion and the fox; virtù and fortuna; the case against mercenaries; the praise of Cesare Borgia; the word Machiavellian

t: Machiavelli wrote for new rulers rather than hereditary ones, and set aside the classical tradition's concern with ideal regimes in favour of the effectual truth of how men live.
He wrote it in 1513, a few months after the Medici regime had arrested, tortured and banished him, and meant it for the Medici; it was printed only in 1532, five years after his death.
Its advice on cruelty, deceit and the keeping of one's word shocked contemporaries, put it on the Index in 1559, and left a lasting mark on the words Machiavellian and politics.
dyk: After Napoleon's defeat at Waterloo, his extensive written comments on The Prince were found in the emperor's coach and taken by the Prussian military.
ev: Machiavelli writes a version of the treatise, under the Latin title De Principatibus
Giuliano di Lorenzo de' Medici, for whom the book was first intended, dies
The Prince is printed, five years after Machiavelli's death, with the permission of Pope Clement VII
Paul IV places The Prince and the Discourses on Livy on the Index, nearly stopping their publication in Catholic areas except France
Innocent Gentillet publishes his Discourse against Machiavelli in Geneva
Frederick the Great's Anti-Machiavel is published, written under the guidance of Voltaire

sections.origins:
Niccolò Machiavelli, an Italian diplomat and political philosopher, wrote The Prince in the form of an instruction guide for new princes. His correspondence shows that a version was being written in 1513, under the Latin title De Principatibus (Of Principalities). The Medici had regained control of Florence the year before, and a few months before the writing Machiavelli had been arrested, tortured and banished by the incoming Medici regime. He discussed the work for a long time with his friend Francesco Vettori, whom he wanted to pass it on and commend it to the Medici.

The book was first intended for Giuliano di Lorenzo de' Medici, who died in 1516, and it came to be dedicated to Lorenzo di Piero de' Medici, grandson of Lorenzo the Magnificent, whose uncle Giovanni became Pope Leo X in 1513. In the dedicatory letter Machiavelli calls himself a humble servant and says the book holds knowledge gained from his political experiences, his hardships and dangers, and from the actions of great men. It is not certain that any of the Medici read the work before it was printed. It belongs to the mirrors for princes genre, yet its author appears to distance it from the classical works of political philosophy, which he viewed as too concerned with the ideal regime.
sections.content:
After the dedicatory letter to Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino, the treatise runs to 26 chapters. In its first sentence Machiavelli uses the word stato, state, to cover all forms of organisation of supreme political power, whether republican or princely. He distinguishes new princedoms from established hereditary ones, which he says are much easier to rule, and treats the ways a new prince may rise: by virtue (virtù), by fortune, by crimes, or by the support of his fellow citizens. Chapters 12 to 14 turn to arms; he stands strongly against mercenaries and auxiliary troops, and holds that a prince's main concern should be war, or the preparation for it.

Chapters 15 to 19 take up the qualities of a prince. Machiavelli says he prefers to go to the effectual truth of the thing rather than to the imagination of it, and writes that it is far safer to be feared than loved if a prince cannot be both. He advises a prince to keep his word only when it suits him while maintaining the appearance of reliability, and compares force to the lion and deception to the fox. Chapter 25 treats fortune, which he says judges only half of our actions, and the final chapter is an exhortation to the Medici to seize Italy and free her from the barbarians, using Italian armies.
sections.making:
Machiavelli's letters show that the work was being written in 1513, but the dating of its composition has been much debated, since some interpreters believe he changed his views between The Prince and the Discourses on Livy. Hans Baron argued that he must have changed his mind dramatically in favour of free republics after writing The Prince. Harvey Mansfield and Nathan Tarcov, in the introduction to their translation of the Discourses, state that there are no discrepancies and that the two are a pair of works, not much different, if at all, in time of composition. William Connell views the composition as a lengthy process, with ideas revised from 1513 to 1515.

The title Il Principe differs from the original Latin De Principatibus and appeared after the book was published in 1532. Scholars possess no manuscript in Machiavelli's own handwriting. He describes the contents as an unembellished summary of his knowledge of the nature of princes and of the actions of great men, based not only on reading but, unusually, on real experience. He says he did not fill the book with rounded periods or big words. This has been read as a distancing from traditional rhetoric, though there are echoes of classical rhetoric, such as the lion and the fox, which according to Zerba most likely came from Cicero.
sections.reception:
The kinds of political behaviour that Machiavelli discusses with approval in The Prince were regarded as shocking by contemporaries, and its immorality is still a subject of serious discussion. Controversy had swirled about his writings since the first appearance of The Prince in manuscript. According to Robert Bireley, about fifteen editions of The Prince and nineteen of the Discourses, with French translations of each, were in circulation before Paul IV placed them on the Index in 1559, a measure that nearly stopped publication in Catholic areas except France. Cardinal Reginald Pole wrote that he found it to be a book written by an enemy of the human race. He also reported that Thomas Cromwell spoke highly of it and that it had influenced Henry VIII, and a copy was possessed by Charles V.

In 1576 the Huguenot Innocent Gentillet published his Discourse against Machiavelli in Geneva, accusing him of atheism and calling his works the Koran of the courtiers; he also questioned the effectiveness of immoral strategies. Counter Reformation writers including Giovanni Botero and Justus Lipsius criticised Machiavelli but followed him in many ways, and tended to cite Tacitus instead, a pretence known as Tacitism. In the 16th century Catholic writers associated him with the Protestants, whereas Protestant authors saw him as Italian and Catholic.
sections.survival:
The Prince was printed in 1532, five years after Machiavelli's death, with the permission of the Medici pope Clement VII. Scholars possess no manuscript in his own hand. The new technology of the printing press helped his ideas on honour and power reach political leaders throughout the modern West, and French translations circulated before the Index of 1559 nearly stopped publication in Catholic areas other than France. The Tridentine Index of 1564 again condemned his works.

Later centuries read the treatise in many translations. English versions include W. K. Marriot's of 1908, Allan Gilbert's of 1958, George Bull's for Penguin of 1961, Harvey Mansfield's of 1985, Robert M. Adams's Norton Critical Edition of 1992, Stephen J. Milner's of 1995, Tim Parks's of 2009 and William J. Connell's of 2015, and a Spanish edition carries commentaries by Napoleon. Napoleon's comments on the book were found in his coach after Waterloo and taken by the Prussian military.
sections.legacy:
The Prince is the most remembered of Machiavelli's works and the one most responsible for the later pejorative use of the word Machiavellian; it even contributed to the modern negative connotations of politics and politician in Western countries. It is sometimes claimed to be one of the first works of modern philosophy, one in which practical effect counts for more than any abstract ideal, and its worldview came into direct conflict with the dominant Catholic and scholastic doctrines of the time on politics and ethics.

Jean Bodin, Francis Bacon, Spinoza, Rousseau, Hume, Edward Gibbon and Adam Smith are among those who noted the importance of his realism, and he is thought to have influenced Montaigne, Descartes, Hobbes, Locke and Montesquieu. On the English stage he appears in the prologue of Christopher Marlowe's The Jew of Malta, and Shakespeare's Othello, Macbeth and Richard III have characters of the type called the stage Machiavel. Seventeenth-century English republicanism was strongly influenced by his thought, as were, it is often proposed, most of the Founding Fathers of the American Revolution. Frederick the Great of Prussia criticised him in an Anti-Machiavel published in 1740, and in the 20th century Benito Mussolini wrote a discourse on the book while Joseph Stalin annotated his own copy.

summary: The Prince is Machiavelli's short treatise of advice to new rulers, written from 1513 after the Medici had banished him and printed in 1532. Its break with the classical ideal regime, and its approval of cruelty and deceit where needed, drew condemnation and shaped the word Machiavellian.
